title: Older Than Hell
subtitle: How a god becomes a demon
blurb: A storm god, a goddess, a Persian fury and a Roman door: the older, holier lives of the names in the catalogue.

segments.t: Last night I let you admire the animals. Tonight I ask where they came from, and for that we leave the cellar. Stand on a beach with me instead. The coast of Canaan, more than three thousand years ago. The sky is turning the colour of a bruise.

The people on this shore are watching the same cloud, and they are not afraid. They are relieved. Because someone is riding that cloud. He carries thunder like a club and lightning like a spear, and when he arrives, the wheat lives. They call him the Rider of the Clouds. His title is Baal. It simply means lord.

We know this from his own worshippers. Behind you is their city, Ugarit, on what is now the Syrian coast. It burned, and its clay tablets lay in the ruins until a farmer's plough struck stone in nineteen twenty-eight. On them, Baal fights the sea, dies, and returns with the rain. Now remember the first night. A hoarse king who comes as a cat and a toad. Tonight, how gods become demons.

Here is the mechanism. When one religion defeats another, the old gods are not deleted. Deleting a god is hard. People know his name, his mountain, his feast days. So you do something cleverer. You keep him, and you demote him. You say, yes, he is real. He is just not what you were told.

You can watch it happen in a single word. In Hebrew, the ninety-sixth Psalm says the gods of the nations are idols. Then, in the last centuries before the common era, Jewish scholars in Egypt put their scriptures into Greek. That translation is called the Septuagint. And in the Greek, the word is different.
For the Lord is great, and greatly to be praised: he is terrible above all gods. For all the gods of the heathen are devils: but the Lord made the heavens.
segments.src: Septuagint, Psalm 95 (96 in English Bibles), Brenton translation (1851)

segments.t: Devils. In the Greek, daimonia. Not nothing. Not carved wood. Somebody. The early Christians inherited that verse and leaned on it hard. Your neighbour's god is real, and he works for the other side. A conquered god makes an excellent devil. He arrives with a name and a reputation already attached. So let us open some case files.

Case one, the lord himself. In the Hebrew Bible, Baal is the rival. On Mount Carmel, Elijah challenges his priests to call down fire. Baal loses. Losing is the start of his second career. By the time the name reaches an English catalogue it is spelled Bael, and the storm is gone. The road is not fully mapped, but almost nobody doubts it. I think the hoarse voice is the saddest part. He used to be thunder.

The name has a more famous child. In the Book of Kings there is a god called Baal Zebub, lord of the flies. Many scholars suspect a Hebrew sneer at a real title, Baal the Prince. Likely, not proven. By the Gospels, Beelzebub is the prince of devils. And, curiously, he is not among the seventy-two. Baal's most famous descendant never got an entry.

Case two is crueller. Sail down this coast to Tyre and Sidon, the cities of the Phoenicians. Their great goddess is Astarte. Lady of love and war, close kin to Ishtar of Babylon. The Bible calls her Ashtoreth, and reports with disgust that Solomon himself, in old age, went after her. In the plural, her images are the Ashtaroth.

Now look in your grimoire, at a seal you collected on the third night. Astaroth. A duke. He. A hurtful angel on a dragon, with breath you were warned about. Somewhere between Sidon and the demon lists of Europe, it seems, a Hebrew plural was taken for a proper name, and a goddess became a man. She did not only lose her temples. She lost even her sex in the translation.

threshold.q: So, my first question tonight. A god is beaten, renamed, and filed under devils. Is he still a god?

opts.label: Yes. Gods don't resign
opts.reply: Then you agree with the people who demoted them, which is the strange part. Nobody in this story says the old gods are gone. The winners insist they are still there, still powerful, still listening. They only changed the label on the door. You and the inquisitors would get along better than either of you would like.

opts.label: He never was one
opts.reply: Tidy. And notice what follows from it. If Baal was only ever a story about rain, then Bael is only a story about a story, and what we are tracing tonight is how stories behave under pressure. I think that is a perfectly good thing to spend a night on. Stories under pressure is most of history.

opts.label: Depends who's counting
opts.reply: The careful answer, and the one the sources support. In Ugarit he is a god. In the Book of Kings he is a rival. In the Greek Psalms he is a devil. Same name, three ledgers. A historian does not get to pick one. A historian writes down who was holding the pen each time.

segments.t: Keep your answer. Case three travelled furthest. You met Asmoday on the fifth night, the king with three heads. His past begins in ancient Persia, in the religion of Zoroaster, where the demon of wrath is called Aeshma. Most scholars think his name, with the Persian word for demon on the end, travelled west and became Asmodeus. Most, not all. That exact compound is not found in the Persian scriptures, and some specialists reject the link. Likely, then. Not certain.

What is certain is where he turns up next. The Book of Tobit, a Jewish tale some two centuries older than the Gospels. A young woman named Sarah has been married seven times. Each bridegroom has died on the wedding night, killed by a demon. Asmodeus. The eighth, Tobias, travels with an angel in disguise, whose advice is peculiar. Burn the heart and liver of a fish.
The which smell when the evil spirit had smelled, he fled into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.
segments.src: Book of Tobit, chapter 8, King James Version

segments.t: Routed by fish smoke. Then the rabbis of the Talmud take him up, and he becomes Ashmedai, king of the demons. Solomon has him brought in chains, to learn how to cut the Temple stones without iron. He helps. Then he tricks the king out of his ring, flings him four hundred leagues, and takes his throne. Persian fury, Jewish folktale, and at last the three-headed king in your grimoire. The best-travelled demon in the book.
He appeareth like a Wolf with a Serpents tail, vomiting out of his mouth flames of fire.

That is case four, and it comes with a warning label. Amon, the seventh name in the catalogue. A marquis, with forty legions. A wolf with a serpent's tail, vomiting fire. Ask, and he becomes a man with a raven's head, sometimes with a dog's teeth set in it. He tells all things past and to come. He stirs up feuds, and he reconciles friends who have quarrelled. His seal is in your grimoire now.

Now the name. In Egyptian Thebes, the king of the gods was Amun. It means the hidden one. Greeks called him Ammon, and crossed a desert to question his oracle. Is the wolf the hidden god of Egypt, demoted? Perhaps. The link is suggestive, and it is debated. Others point to Baal Hammon of Carthage. It may be only two names that sound alike. Nobody has the paper trail.
He appeareth in the Form of a Soldier with Red Clothing, riding upon a Red Horse, and having a Crown of Gold upon his head.

Case five, with a better paper trail. Berith, number twenty-eight. A duke, with twenty-six legions. Red soldier, red horse, gold crown, and a voice the book calls clear and subtle. He answers truly about past, present and future. He turns any metal into gold. He gives dignities and confirms them. And the old catalogues add, quite calmly, that he is a liar. I leave you to decide how much of his gold to accept.

His name is in the Book of Judges. After Gideon dies, Israel turns to a god called Baal Berith. His temple stands in the town of Shechem. Berith is Hebrew for covenant. Lord of the Covenant. The god you swore your treaties by. The demon's name is almost certainly his. So the keeper of oaths became a spirit who cannot be trusted. That is not just demotion. That is satire.

threshold.q: Second question. Suppose you could restore one. Hand one fallen god the temple back. Which would it be?

opts.label: Baal, for the storm
opts.reply: I hoped someone would. Imagine him getting his voice back. One clap of thunder over the sea, after three thousand years of being a toad with a sore throat. I cannot promise he would be kind about it. Storm gods are not known for letting things go. But it would be something to hear.

opts.label: Astarte, as herself
opts.reply: A just choice. She has the longest list of grievances. Her name mangled, her sex changed, her temples turned into a warning. I suspect she would want the name corrected before anything else. Gods are particular about names. So, as you have noticed by now, are demons.

opts.label: None. Leave them be
opts.reply: Sensible. A restored god wants things. Festivals, sacrifices, a say in the harvest. A fossil asks for nothing and tells you a great deal. There is a reason museums keep the glass between you and the exhibit, and it is not only to protect the exhibit.

segments.t: Whatever you chose, the last file is about a door. Come in out of the weather, and down. Number forty-six. Bifrons. An earl, with six legions in the printed book, so few that its own editor suspected a slip. He comes first as a monster, and then, when he is told to, as a man. He teaches astrology and geometry, and the virtues of precious stones and woods. And then his entry turns, quietly, to the graveyard.
He changeth Dead Bodies, and putteth them in another place; also he lighteth seeming Candles upon the Graves of the Dead.

Seeming candles. Now his name. Bifrons is plain Latin. It means two-faced. And it was a well-known title of Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who looks both ways at once. The demon is never described with two faces, and nobody can prove the borrowing. But a spirit named for the god of thresholds, who carries the dead across one? I find that hard to call an accident.

He does not work the graveyard alone. Number twenty-six is Bune, a duke with thirty legions. He is a dragon with three heads, one like a dog, one like a gryphon, one like a man, and he speaks in a high and comely voice. He gives riches, wisdom and eloquence. And he changes the place of the dead, the book says, and makes the spirits under him gather upon your tombs.

And number fifty-four, Murmur. A duke, and the book calls him an earl as well, with thirty legions. A warrior riding a gryphon, in a ducal crown, with his ministers going before him sounding great trumpets. He teaches philosophy perfectly. And he constrains the souls of the dead to come and answer questions. His name is only the Latin for a low sound. A whisper, with a brass band in front of it.

Three keepers of the dead. One moves the bodies, one gathers the spirits on the tombs, one makes the souls speak. No lost god stands behind Bune or Murmur that anyone can name. But the office is ancient. That work is older than any church. The book simply kept it on the payroll.

So look at what you are holding. The Lesser Key was copied out in England in the sixteen hundreds, by people who believed they were listing the staff of Hell. Without meaning to, they were also building a museum. Under the seventeenth-century ink there is a Canaanite storm. A Phoenician goddess. Persian wrath. Perhaps an Egyptian mystery. A Roman door.

These names were once said kindly. By a farmer who wanted rain. By a bride. By somebody in a doorway at the turn of the year. The prayers stopped, and the names kept travelling, stranger at every border, until they came to rest in a catalogue. Every demon is a fossil of somebody's prayer. You do not have to believe in anything to find that a little haunting.

Tomorrow, The Men Who Opened the Book. A Dutch doctor who printed a list of demons while defending women accused of witchcraft. An Englishman who reprinted it to show it was all nonsense. And two magicians who came to loathe each other.

Until then. Five more seals are in your grimoire. A wolf, a red soldier, a monster, a dragon and a man with trumpets. And if it rains on your way home tonight, be civil about it. Somebody was very proud of that, once.

glossary.def: A Semitic word meaning lord or master, and the usual title of the Canaanite storm god Hadad. In the Hebrew Bible he is the great rival of Israel's God; in the Lesser Key the name survives as the first spirit, Bael.

A Bronze Age port city on the Syrian coast, destroyed about twelve centuries before the common era. Clay tablets dug up there in the twentieth century preserve the myths of Baal in the words of his own worshippers.
The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Egypt in the third century before the common era. Its Psalms call the gods of other nations daimonia, demons.
The demon of wrath in the Zoroastrian religion of ancient Persia. Widely, though not universally, thought to lie behind the name Asmodeus, the Asmoday of the Lesser Key.
Janus was the Roman god of doorways, beginnings and endings, shown with two faces looking opposite ways. Bifrons, two-faced, was one of his titles, and is also the name of the forty-sixth spirit.
